canonical_statement: For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ let $A_x\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded set with outer measure $<1$. Must there exist an infinite independent set, that is, some infinite $X\subseteq \mathbb{R}$ such that $x\not\in A_y$ for all $x\neq y\in X$?If the sets $A_x$ are closed and have measure $<1$, then must there exist an independent set of size $3$?

must_determine: For clause 1 prove either the full ZFC universal independent-set theorem or a full ZFC counterexample family.
For clause 2 provide/import a verified ZFC proof and the size-3 restriction lemma.
close_branch_A.statement: DIRECT ZFC DETERMINATION: resolve clause 1 in ZFC and retain the established affirmative ZFC resolution of clause 2.

must_determine: A CH counterexample is admissible as one side of an independence proof when all canonical hypotheses are checked, but by itself it is a conditional result rather than a complete ZFC verdict.
Supply the complementary consistency/positive side needed for a genuine independence conclusion.
close_branch_B.statement: INDEPENDENCE CLOSE: prove clause 1 independent of ZFC by giving the required relative-consistency directions/models for the exact bounded outer-measure family statement; clause 2 remains ZFC-affirmative.

definitions: Formal-semantics guard: any Lean or equivalent formalization used in the campaign must be semantically bound back to this canonical statement. Types, endpoint conventions, and degenerate cases may not be guessed; any formal/prose mismatch must be resolved explicitly before claiming closure.

Quantifier-order guard: the quantifiers occur in the order stated and may not be commuted, weakened, or replaced by sampled cases. Salient source phrases include: For every $x\in\mathbb{R}$ let $A_x\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded set with outer measure $<1$; for all $x\neq y\in X$; there exist an infinite independent set; there exist an independent set of size $3$.
Real-domain guard: inequalities, limits, measure, and constants are interpreted over the reals exactly as stated; rational or discrete surrogate domains require a proved equivalence.
Measure guard: preserve the exact measure notion (including outer measure if named), ambient measurable space, positivity/normalization, and whether measurability is an assumption or a conclusion.

Infinitary guard: cardinality, ordinal order type, cofinality, and chromatic cardinal are not interchangeable. Universe/cardinality assumptions and strict/weak inequalities between cardinals must survive formalization.
Independence guard: an independent set contains no edges of the ambient graph on that vertex subset; sparse or low-chromatic substitutes are weaker unless explicitly proved equivalent.

Clause 1 quantifies an arbitrary family (A_x)_{x∈ℝ} where each A_x⊆ℝ is bounded in its own possibly x-dependent interval and has Lebesgue outer measure <1; measurability is not assumed. An independent X satisfies x∉A_y for every distinct x,y∈X.

Clause 2 assumes each A_x is closed and has Lebesgue measure <1. 'An independent set of size 3' means existence of at least three distinct reals forming an independent set; any larger independent set supplies such a triple by restriction.
The closed-set clause is already known affirmatively in ZFC through the cited theorem; a complete contract records/reproduces that proof while separately determining the outer-measure clause.
The family is indexed by every real x. Each A_x is bounded in the standard Bornology.IsBounded sense in ℝ and has outer measure <1; no common bounding interval is required.
Clause 2's known ZFC theorem may be used only after proving the restriction step from an infinite independent set to a 3-element independent subset.
invariants_that_must_survive_every_refor: The canonical statement text is immutable; every proof target must imply exactly that statement (or its literal negation for a negative close).
Every quantifier, domain, hypothesis, strict/non-strict inequality, endpoint, normalization, and parameter dependency survives every reformulation.
Discrete structure is preserved: integrality, distinctness, ordering, multiplicity/set-vs-multiset conventions, and exact cardinalities may not be relaxed silently.
Any asymptotic/eventual claim retains the same limiting variable and full-sequence requirement.
All 2 explicit interrogative clauses (and any declarative requested subclaims) remain jointly in scope until each is resolved.
The index set of the family is all ℝ and boundedness is ordinary bornological boundedness for each A_x separately.
known_traps: QUANTIFIER SLIP: exchanging ∀ and ∃, moving an epsilon/constant after the limiting variable, or replacing “all sufficiently large” by “infinitely many”.
SAMPLED-TO-UNIVERSAL: checking many finite instances and promoting the observation to an unrestricted theorem without a valid finite-reduction theorem.
DOMAIN DRIFT: proving a translated/scaled/relaxed version without an exact map back to the original domain, endpoints, and discrete constraints.
STRENGTH CONFUSION: refuting a stronger folklore conjecture does not refute the canonical claim; proving a weaker statement does not prove it.
PARTIAL-CLOSE TRAP: the source contains 2 explicit questions; solving one or several but not all is a partial result, not a close.
MEASURE NOTION: clause 1 uses outer measure without measurability; clause 2 uses ordinary Lebesgue measure because closed sets are measurable.
DEPENDENCE ORDER: every asymptotic constant and threshold has exactly the parameter dependence fixed in definitions; a constant chosen after the limiting variable or witness family is not uniform.
non_results: A theorem for only a selected finite set of parameter values when the statement is uniform or asymptotic.
A result only on a favorable subsequence, density-one subset, almost-everywhere set, or “generic” family when the canonical statement requires the full sequence/all objects.
A numerical fit, heuristic, Monte Carlo result, floating-point experiment, or finite computation without a proved finite-reduction/transfer theorem to the canonical claim.
A restricted-family result obtained by adding hypotheses not present in the statement, unless those hypotheses are proved without loss of generality for every canonical instance.
A reduction to an equivalent-strength open problem, a tautological rephrasing, or a definition of the requested answer in terms of the original target predicate.
A continuous/real-valued/LP/SDP relaxation without a proved integrality or exact-transfer theorem when the canonical objects are discrete.
A stronger-looking statement in a different normalization/domain that does not formally imply the canonical statement.
Resolving fewer than all parts of the canonical statement (which contains 2 explicit question marks) and calling the problem closed.
Proving one subquestion implies another without establishing the implication under the exact source definitions.
A result only for measurable, analytic, countable, or uniformly bounded families does not settle the arbitrary outer-measure clause.
A CH-only or MA-only theorem may be a component of a set-theoretic independence proof, but one conditional direction alone is not a complete resolution of clause 1.
permitted_background: Definitions and elementary facts in the named mathematical domain, with every imported theorem used only under its exact published/formal hypotheses.

Standard algebraic, combinatorial, analytic, probabilistic, number-theoretic, set-theoretic, and asymptotic lemmas needed to manipulate the objects appearing in the statement; no theorem equivalent in strength to the target may be assumed.

Exact finite computation, SAT/SMT/MILP, interval arithmetic, symbolic algebra, exhaustive enumeration, or custom verified tooling may be used as a lemma/certificate when its finite search space and transfer to the unrestricted claim are proved.
Lean/Mathlib or another proof assistant may certify intermediate and final results; kernel acceptance does not by itself excuse a semantic mismatch with the canonical statement.
Standard real/measure/asymptotic analysis may be used, but pointwise, uniform, almost-everywhere, in-measure, density, limsup, and full-limit conclusions may not be interchanged.
